C0.quote: We study a two-candidate (referred to as A and B) election
C0.note: Two-candidate majority election with costly participation/abstention; equilibrium turnout and Condorcet Jury Theorem.

C1.quote: So we have a rather complete characterization of equilibria, or at least
C1.note: Main results: existence, limit points, stability of turnout equilibria and Jury/non-Jury theorems at equilibrium limits; Sec. 6.1 adds a numerical simulation on a synthetic example (Example 5). Winning probability of the better candidate is analysed as a property of equilibria, not as performance against a welfare/distortion objective (consistent with C5.1 = N).

C2.1.value: votes (vote for one of the two candidates or abstain); 'active votes' for A and B
C2.1.quote: number of active votes for A (and likewise for B)

C2.2.quote: each voter is to vote for one of the two candidates
C2.2.note: Single vote for one of two candidates, with an abstention option; majority rule over active votes.

C2.3.quote: supporter of A (prefers A, i.e., A ≻i B) or a supporter
C2.3.note: Voters have a type (cost ci, preferred candidate Ti) and utility 1 for favourite candidate.

C2.4.quote: strategy profile is therefore a mapping v from the type
C2.4.note: Type (ci, Ti) is separate from the action in {vote for Ti, abstain}; voting for the less preferred candidate is noted as strictly dominated.

C3.1.quote: voters abstain if their participation cost is greater than their
C3.1.note: Strategic element is only the participation decision (abstaining instead of submitting a vote for the preferred candidate) in every analysis; votes actually cast always follow the held preference. Could alternatively be read as NONE if abstention is not considered a differing input.

C4.1.note: C2.2 coded OTH only (single vote with abstention), so applicability condition not met. The paper does set utility 1 for the favourite candidate.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.quote: the Winning Probability of A in profile c of election
C5.1.note: Results evaluate the probability that the better/majority-preferred candidate A wins (Jury theorems), which is not framed as welfare, efficiency, satisfaction, representation, proportionality or distortion. Borderline with representation of the majority.

VOT.quote_behav: each player picks an action that maximizes her expected utility
VOT.quote_info: the only private information a voter has (other than the type
VOT.note: Voters decide to vote or abstain by comparing cost with (perceived) pivotality; they know the common type distribution (prior) and, in PPMs, expected turnout and margin, but not others' realized types.

CAN.note: Candidates A and B are only alternatives.

C8.1.note: Bayes-Nash equilibrium for the Calculus of Voting; 'election equilibrium' with heuristic perceived pivotality models (BND); stability of equilibria (Theorem 9) is defined via simultaneous best-response dynamics converging to the equilibrium (App. D, Def. 11) (ITER).

C8.1.reason: Stability, a main result, is defined through best-response dynamics ('a best response by few agents will get closer to Q... until convergence'), so ITER applies in addition to BNE and BND.
